messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 56

# The Weight of the Waiting Room

Marcus is a 51-year-old school principal who, by most external measures, appears to be exactly the kind of man who holds things together. He is the first car in the parking lot each morning, the one who knows every student's name, the one teachers call when a situation feels impossible. He has built his professional identity around steadiness. Which is why, he says quietly, what happened three years ago feels like a particular kind of betrayal — not just of his body, but of everything he thought he was.

At 48, Marcus was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia. He had gone to his physician for what he assumed was persistent fatigue from overwork — he had recently buried his wife of nineteen years, who died of a stroke, and had thrown himself into his job to survive the grief. The diagnosis arrived instead. He remembers the oncologist's face before she spoke, the particular stillness of it, and says that image surfaces without warning still — at faculty meetings, in the cereal aisle, in the dark before sleep arrives.

The treatment was aggressive. Four rounds of induction chemotherapy, a bone marrow transplant, months in an isolation room where the window faced a concrete wall. He describes lying in that hospital bed not knowing whether the nausea or the terror was worse, listening to the sounds of the ward at night, calculating odds in his head the way a person counts sheep. He had no wife to sit beside him. His adult daughter flew in when she could, but she had young children, and Marcus told her — repeatedly, insistently — that he was fine, that she should go home. He spent a great deal of time alone with the hum of IV machines and the certainty that he was going to die.

He did not die. His oncologist calls him a success story. Marcus uses different language.

Now, three years into remission, he functions — impressively, from the outside. He runs a school of 600 students. He attends every basketball game. He mentors new teachers with genuine care. But he lives, he says, in a body he no longer fully trusts, in a future he cannot bring himself to picture. Every three months he sits in the oncology waiting room for bloodwork, and in the forty-eight hours before each appointment, he stops sleeping. He checks his skin for bruises. He avoids his daughter's calls because he doesn't want her to hear something in his voice that he cannot name.

At school, he has developed what his assistant principal calls an "intensity" — a hypervigilance about safety drills, about sick children being sent home, about anything that feels medically adjacent. A student with a nosebleed in the hallway last fall sent him into his office, door closed, heart hammering, for twenty minutes before he could compose himself enough to return. He told no one.

He rarely speaks about the illness to colleagues. When a teacher recently mentioned a family member's cancer diagnosis, Marcus excused himself from the conversation and stood in the men's room gripping the sink until the feeling passed. He describes this feeling as a wave — not of sadness exactly, but of something colder, a sense of the floor dissolving beneath him.

He sleeps four or five hours most nights, wakes from dreams he cannot always recall but that leave him damp and disoriented. He has started running at five in the morning, partly for his health, he says, and partly because the movement keeps the thoughts from assembling. He has not been on a date since his wife died. He tells himself this is loyalty, but in quieter moments he admits it may be something else — a reluctance to let anyone close to something so fragile, so recently almost gone.

He came to therapy, he says, because his daughter asked him to. He is not sure, he adds, that he has anything left worth saving. Then he corrects himself, embarrassed. He didn't mean it that way.
